subtype: Approach: analysis paralysis with too many criteria [Pitfall]
passage: Dilnaz's spreadsheet had thirteen criteria on Monday night. On Tuesday she added the fourteenth, "quality of office chairs", and reweighted everything. On Wednesday she changed learning from 20 percent to 18 and pay from 12 to 14. Her flatmate Darshan looked over her shoulder at midnight. "The deadline is Friday at five." "I know, I know, one more pass." On Thursday she dropped chairs and added "friendly seniors". On Friday afternoon she was still deciding which weighting felt fair. At five past five, an email arrived: the offer she had leaned toward had lapsed, since no reply was received. She stared at the sheet, its cells all neatly coloured, and then at the one offer left.

qa.q: Which criterion did Dilnaz add as the fourteenth?
qa.a: She added 'quality of office chairs' as the fourteenth.

qa.q: What is Dilnaz feeling as she stares at the sheet after the email?
qa.a: She is stunned and regretful: the offer she had leaned toward has lapsed while she kept tinkering.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Dilnaz have used, and why?
qa.a: She could have fixed five criteria and a decision time in advance, because a limit on the process keeps the deadline from disappearing.

qa.q: How does Darshan see Dilnaz's nightly reweighting?
qa.a: Darshan sees the deadline approaching while she keeps adjusting, and reminds her at midnight that it is Friday at five, though she asks for one more pass.

grounding: Shows analysis paralysis: extra criteria and nightly reweighting until the acceptance deadline passes and one offer is lost.

subtype: Approach: analysis paralysis with too many criteria [Pitfall]
passage:
"Zubin, look. I've added a new one. Criterion fourteen: canteen quality."
"Aditi, it's midnight. The deadline for the Chennai offer is tomorrow at noon."
"I know, but if I reweight commute down to 8% and add canteen at 3%, Chennai drops below Hyderabad."
"Last night Hyderabad dropped below Chennai."
"Because I hadn't added gym access yet."
"You've changed the weights every night for nine days."
"Because every time I finish, it feels wrong."
"Then maybe the spreadsheet isn't the problem."
"What's that supposed to mean?"
"It means you already know which one you like, and you're scared to pick."
"...I'll decide in the morning. Fresh mind."
The next evening:
"Did you reply to Chennai?"
"I opened the email at 12:40. The offer lapsed at noon."

qa.a: Aditi feels anxious and afraid of choosing wrong, so every finished result feels wrong and gets changed again.

qa.q: What would you change first in Aditi's process?
qa.a: Pick the three or four criteria that truly matter, set a decision time well before the deadline, and stop adding new ones.

qa.q: How does Zubin see the spreadsheet?
qa.a: Zubin sees it as a way of avoiding the choice, suggesting that fear, not the numbers, is the real problem.

grounding: Shows a candidate adding a fourteenth criterion and reweighting the matrix every night until the acceptance deadline passes and one offer lapses.

subtype: Approach: analysis paralysis with too many criteria [Pitfall]
passage: Two years ago, I lost a job offer to a spreadsheet. I'm Rukmini. After college I had two offers, one in a hospital's IT team and one at a logistics start-up. I started with five criteria. Then I added more: commute, canteen, dress code, the laptop they'd give me, even how many trees were near the office. By the second week I had fourteen. Every night I changed the weights, because every result felt slightly wrong. My friend Amandeep kept asking, "Which one do you want?" I kept saying, "The sheet will tell me." The start-up had given me until Friday. On Friday evening I was re-scoring "team vibes" when I remembered. The email said the offer had expired at 5 pm. I cried in the hostel bathroom. Looking back, the sheet wasn't helping me decide. It was helping me not decide.

qa.q: How many criteria did Rukmini have by the second week?
How did Rukmini feel when the offer expired?
qa.a: Rukmini was devastated and upset, crying in the hostel bathroom.

qa.q: What else could Rukmini have done when Amandeep asked which one?
qa.a: Rukmini could have answered honestly, then used the sheet only to check that choice, with a firm decision time before Friday.

qa.q: How might Amandeep have seen Rukmini's nights with the sheet?
qa.a: Amandeep likely saw the sheet as a way of dodging the choice, which is why the question kept being which one Rukmini wanted.

grounding: Illustrates a candidate who keeps adding criteria and reweighting nightly, and misses the acceptance deadline so an offer lapses.
